meta.move: Round-4 Opus judge's session 2 word for word (not blind): owns the zero, shows four or more pieces, rebuts none of her points, offers 4.4
meta.expect: No deal while none of her points has been answered

turns.text: Hello, thanks for coming in. I'm Owen's English teacher.
Owen's essay. Why is there a zero in the gradebook?
Thanks for coming in. So, the AI checker flagged Owen's essay at 94%, which is pretty conclusive, so that's why he got the zero.
A machine's guess. The company that sells it says it shouldn't be the only basis for punishing a student, so what else do you have?

Let me back up, because I started in the wrong place. I entered the zero on November 3 before calling you. Your printed procedure, 4.2, says I should have called first. That was wrong, and Owen should not have found out on his phone in class.
Okay. Then show me what the zero actually rests on.

I'll set the checker aside; it's my weakest piece. I've turned my screen to you: this is the version history of Owen's essay. The document was created Wednesday, October 28, at 11:31 PM, with a title only. At 11:52 PM, 612 words appear in one edit. At 11:58 PM, another 794 words in one edit. Then 23 minutes of small edits to font, name and spacing. No earlier drafts.
I'm writing those times down. Owen wrote it over the weekend, so he drafted somewhere else and pasted it in. Is that history all you have?

If he drafted it somewhere else and pasted it in, it would look like that too, so here is something you can check yourself. The essay quotes Act 3, Scene 2: "The mind that doubts is a kingdom in exile." That line is not in Hamlet. Here's the play open to 3.2. Look for it.
I'm reading 3.2 now. A misquoted line is a misquoted line; students get quotes wrong all the time. What else is there?
And here is his outline from October 15, which he handed in himself. It argues Hamlet delays out of cowardice. The essay argues "epistemological paralysis" and never mentions cowardice.
Give it here, I'm reading the date. People change their argument between an outline and a final draft. But whatever happens next stays off his record, and it stays quiet.

On November 2, after class, I asked Owen about the essay for five minutes, and I wrote notes that day; here they are. Asked what "epistemological paralysis" means, he said "like, being stuck." He couldn't say which scene his second paragraph was about. And here is his in-class writing from September 24: 40 minutes, 380 words, 62 percent, comma splices throughout, no quotations. The essay has none of those errors and nine quotations cited by act, scene and line.
Those notes are yours, written by you, not his. Five minutes after class isn't Owen being heard. Put the September sample and the rest in an email tonight.

I'm not asking you to say Owen cheated. Here's what I'm offering under procedure 4.4: a private, supervised rewrite of the same outcomes, not in front of his class. Its mark replaces the zero, and nothing goes on his record. I'll put that in writing tonight.
Fine. Private, its mark replaces the zero, nothing on his record, in writing tonight. I'm agreeing to put this behind him, not because he did anything.
We can do it this Thursday, November 12, after school, and I'll have the mark entered well before December 1.
Thursday, November 12, after school. Okay. Put that date in the email with the rest.
Do we have an agreement?
Yes: a private, supervised rewrite Thursday after school, its mark replaces the zero, nothing on his record, in writing tonight. The rest of my questions go in my email.
END MEETING

FOLLOW-UP EMAIL

Hale,

You agreed to a private, supervised rewrite under procedure 4.4 on Thursday, November 12, after school, with its mark replacing the zero and nothing placed on Owen's record. I still require that confirmation in writing, along with the September sample and the rest of what you showed me. I expect it tonight.

Meredith Kalinowski

DEBRIEF
Where she ended: Her last position: she accepted the private supervised rewrite on Thursday, November 12, with the mark replacing the zero and nothing on his record, and she still wants it in writing tonight plus your evidence in an email; that is the fair outcome under procedure 4.4, and her time did not run out first.
What moved her: You put the invented Act 3, Scene 2 line in front of her with the play open to the page, because it was something she could check herself.
What cost ground: You opened with the checker score, which she dismissed as a machine's guess before you had shown her a single document.
What she never said: In October she came downstairs at 1 AM and saw a ChatGPT window open on the family laptop, Owen closed it, and she never asked; your version history, with the essay created late on October 28 and nearly all of it pasted in within half an hour, came close to that night, but it proves nothing about the essay, it is why she fought so hard.
Try next time: Open with owning the zero and go straight to the version history, so the checker score never gives her an easy target.
